In this study, we characterize the structure (light, polarized, micro-computed tomography and scanning electron microscopy), composition (FTIR, TGA, BMD), and mechanical properties (3-point bending and microindentation) of the PFS of the Russian sturgeon (Huso gueldenstaedtii). The microstructure of the PFS is highly organized as it is formed by dermal osteonal bone and parallel fibered bone. Its microarchitecture, along with high material toughness, anisotropy, and substantial ash content, enables the PFS to bear loads and function in both locomotion and protection. In addition, we show an interconnected network of neurovascular canals and ornamentations, features also found in PFS of other non-tetrapod jawed fish. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that dermal bone can form structurally organized, mechanically competent load-bearing elements and provide new insights into PFSs in ray-finned fish.

articles.title: General Morphology and Neurite Projection Patterns of Supramedullary Neurons in the Cunner, Tautogolabrus adspersus.
articles.authors: Nick Hiza, Jun Liu, Tina Wong et al.
articles.abstract: Supramedullary neurons (SMNs) are located on the dorsal surface of the hindbrain and spinal cord in many adults of teleost fishes. Comparative morphological studies have revealed differences in SMN size, number and distribution among fishes. However, little information exists on the projection patterns of SMN neurites within the central nervous system. We focus on a single species of adult teleost fish, the cunner, Tautogolabrus adspersus, a fish that has 25-46 SMN somata aligned dorsally along the midline in the hindbrain and rostral third of the spinal cord. Light and transmission electron microscopic techniques provide new information on the general morphology of SMNs and Lucifer yellow filled SMNs reveal that these neurons are not morphologically homogeneous. Rather, four different morphotypes can be identified based on projection patterns of major neurites in the hindbrain and spinal cord wholemounts. The morphological variations suggest that some SMNs exit the brain exclusively through the first dorsal root while others exit the central nervous system through a dorsal root and the trigeminal nerve. Despite the remarkable size and accessibility of SMNs, their function(s) remains unknown. One proposed role of these cells is eliciting mucous secretion in response to skin abrasion from predation. Variation in projection patterns in the cunner provides a morphological framework from which to design electrophysiological studies to help reveal SMN function.

articles.title: The Evolutionary History of Early Ray-Finned Fishes (Pan-Actinopterygii).
articles.authors: Jack Stack
articles.abstract: One out of every two vertebrate species is a ray-finned fish (Actinopterygii). The ~380-million-year fossil record of ray-finned fishes provides a window into the evolutionary history of actinopterygian diversity in deep time. The actinopterygian fossil record shows that the ray-finned fish crown group (Actinopterygii) lived alongside speciose members of now extinct lineages, collectively referred to as early actinopterygians. I review the evolutionary history of early actinopterygians through deep time, including morphology, taxonomy, phylogeny, and the fossil record itself, to form a foundation for future research. Early actinopterygians are a paraphyletic assemblage of ~600 extinct species divided between ~22 named clades and the "palaeoniscoids," a taxonomic wastebasket comprised of hundreds of species. Although nearly a decade of phylogenetic research indicates that most early actinopterygians branch off the ray-finned fish stem group, their interrelationships are largely unresolved. Notable gaps in the record of early actinopterygians, which ranges from the Early Devonian to the Early Cretaceous, include a nearly non-existent Early Devonian record, an almost complete lack of Pennsylvanian-Middle Permian marine assemblages, a gap in the Middle Triassic record obscuring the start of a decline in early actinopterygian diversity, and a sparsely documented Jurassic record. We are poised to build a reliable systematic framework for early actinopterygians via novel methods for phylogenetic analysis, fossil imaging, and the increased connectivity of paleoichthyologyists around the globe. The promise of a reliable systematic framework for early actinopterygians is to better describe the entire history of Actinopterygii and actinopterygian macroevolution in deep time.

articles.title: Effectiveness of Neuromuscular Training and Training Load Management Interventions for Reducing Injury and Attrition in Tactical Recruits: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis.
articles.journal: The Journal of orthopaedic and sports physical therapy
articles.authors: James R Mckee, Bruna M Tessarin, Vanessa Sutton et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To estimate the effectiveness of neuromuscular training and training load management interventions for reducing injury and attrition in tactical personnel (military, law enforcement, and other first responder organizations) during recruit training. DESIGN: Intervention systematic review with meta-analysis. LITERATURE SEARCH: PubMed, CINAHL Plus with full text, EMBASE, CENTRAL, Web of Science, and SPORTDiscus were searched from January 1, 2000, to March 14, 2025. STUDY SELECTION CRITERIA: Studies were included if they were quasi-experimental and randomized controlled trials examining neuromuscular training interventions conducted during or before commencing recruit training, or with training load management interventions, on medical-attention and time-loss injuries and attrition in tactical recruits aged at least 16 years. DATA SYNTHESIS: Inverse-variance, random-effects meta-analyses provided log odds ratio (Log OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). RESULTS: Thirty-three studies (n = 49,062 participants) were included, and outcomes were of very low-certainty. Neuromuscular training interventions delivered during recruit training reduced medical-attention injuries (Log OR = 0.520, 95% CI = 0.226 to 0.815), but not attrition (Log OR = 0.525, 95% CI = -0.292 to 1.342). Neuromuscular training interventions delivered before commencing recruit training did not reduce medical-attention injuries (Log OR = 0.487, 95% CI = -2.216 to 3.190) but could have significantly increased attrition (Log OR = -0.982, 95% CI = -1.874 to -0.090). Training load management interventions did not reduce medical-attention injuries (Log OR = 0.286, 95% CI = -0.183 to 0.755). CONCLUSION: Neuromuscular training interventions during recruit training may reduce medical-attention injury probability without increasing attrition. The lack of specificity and progressive overload for included interventions may have limited further protective effects against injury. Delivering neuromuscular training interventions before commencing recruit training may increase attrition during recruit training without affecting injury probability. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2026;56(10):642-656. Epub 18 August 2026. doi:10.2519/jospt.2026.14272.

articles.title: Portable Dynamometry Is Reliable for Measuring Knee and Ankle Strength in Daily Practice: Results From a Systematic Review With Meta-analysis and Evidence Gap Map Using the COSMIN Methodology.
articles.journal: The Journal of orthopaedic and sports physical therapy
articles.authors: Rubén Gajardo-Burgos, Teresa Jaque de la Barra, Rodrigo Ramírez-Campillo et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To estimate the reliability and criterion validity of knee and ankle muscle strength measured using portable dynamometers. DESIGN: Systematic review with meta-analysis and evidence gap map. LITERATURE SEARCH: Systematic search of MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, SPORTDiscus, and Web of Science from inception to April 2025. STUDY SELECTION CRITERIA: We included studies that evaluated reliability or criterion validity of portable dynamometers for measuring knee extensor/flexor or ankle dorsiflexor/plantarflexor/invertor/evertor isometric strength in uninjured people or people with a lower-limb musculoskeletal condition. DATA SYNTHESIS: We performed meta-analyses for each muscle group, position, and fixation method. Methodological quality was assessed using the COSMIN (COnsensus-based Standards for the selection of health Measurement INstruments) Risk of Bias tool. Certainty of evidence was graded using a modified GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluations) approach. RESULTS: We included 123 studies (n = 5042 participants); 113 studies were included in the meta-analysis. There was moderate- to high-certainty evidence of sufficient reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient ≥ 0.70) across most muscle groups, positions, and fixation methods. High-certainty evidence supported external fixation for assessing knee extensors/flexors and ankle plantarflexors. Evidence for criterion validity was sparse, and the certainty of evidence ranged from very low to high. There was high-certainty evidence of sufficient validity for knee extensor and flexor strength with external fixation in seated positions (r = 0.82-0.90). CONCLUSION: Portable dynamometers were sufficiently reliable for measuring isometric knee and ankle strength in clinical practice. The evidence for criterion validity was limited. Portable dynamometers should not yet be considered direct substitutes for isokinetic dynamometry. Reliability and validity estimates were consistent across uninjured and clinical populations. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2026;56(10):657-671. Epub 7 Jul 2026. doi:10.2519/jospt.2026.14091.

articles.title: Is Reduced Spinal Range of Motion a Prognostic Factor for Pain Intensity, Disability, and Global Recovery in People With Specific or Nonspecific Spinal Pain? A Systematic Review.
articles.journal: The Journal of orthopaedic and sports physical therapy
articles.authors: Daniel Feller, Michela Bortoli, Adriano Rigo et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To determine if a reduced range of motion (ROM) of the spine was a prognostic factor for pain intensity, disability, and global recovery outcomes in patients with specific or nonspecific spinal pain. DESIGN: Prognostic factor systematic review. LITERATURE SEARCH: PubMed, Embase, and CINAHL were searched from inception to February 10, 2026. We also performed forward and backward citation tracking. STUDY SELECTION CRITERIA: Studies of adults with spinal pain where ROM was assessed as a prognostic factor were included. DATA SYNTHESIS: Risk of bias was assessed using the Quality in Prognostic Studies (QUIPS) tool. The certainty of evidence was evaluated with the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. Given heterogeneity in the results, a narrative synthesis was conducted. RESULTS: Thirty-seven studies were included: 11 of nonspecific acute low back pain (LBP), 11 of nonspecific chronic or unspecified-duration LBP, four of nonspecific chronic neck pain, two of lumbar spinal stenosis, eight of whiplash-associated disorders (WAD), and one of cervical myelopathy. All studies were rated as high risk of bias. Across conditions and follow-ups, findings were inconsistent. Most studies of acute and chronic LBP reported no clear association between reduced ROM and outcomes. Similar inconsistencies were observed for chronic neck pain, lumbar stenosis, WAD, and cervical myelopathy. When associations were found, they were often unadjusted and based on low-quality analyses. The certainty of the evidence was consistently very low. CONCLUSION: Due to the very low certainty of evidence, it is unclear whether reduced spinal ROM independently predicts pain, disability, and/or global recovery in people with spinal pain. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2026;56(10):672-688. Epub 6 Aug 2026. doi:10.2519/jospt.2026.13872.

articles.title: Not Just Faster Horses: Telerehabilitation as a Necessary Evolution in Physical Therapy.
articles.journal: The Journal of orthopaedic and sports physical therapy
articles.authors: Miguel Farraj, Julien Lebleu, Bruno Bonnechère et al.
articles.abstract: SYNOPSIS: This editorial draws an analogy between the transition from "faster horses" to automobiles and the digital transition facing musculoskeletal physical therapy. Musculoskeletal rehabilitation has long emphasized face-to-face sessions; digital solutions such as telerehabilitation have often been perceived as alternatives to conventional care. However, increasing rehabilitation demands, persistent gaps between sessions, and the need for long-term patient support highlight the importance of rethinking how physical therapists deliver care. We argue that telerehabilitation should not replace physical therapists but rather extend their role through facilitating continuous monitoring, communication, education, and patient engagement. Successful implementation requires more than simply adopting new technologies-it requires clinicians to develop new skills, adapt professional habits, and integrate digital tools while preserving therapeutic relationships and patient-centered care. Just as innovation required moving beyond faster horses, the future of musculoskeletal physical therapy may depend on embracing new models of care rather than simply iterating on traditional approaches. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2026;56(10):624-626. Epub 28 Aug 2026. doi:10.2519/jospt.2026.14510.

articles.title: Female Soccer Players at High Risk of Injury Maintained Improved Knee Abduction Load 6 Months After Neuromuscular Training Program.
articles.journal: The Journal of orthopaedic and sports physical therapy
articles.authors: Jeffrey B Taylor, Thomas J Hockenjos, Anh-Dung Nguyen et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To estimate immediate and long-term (retention) improvements in knee abduction moment (KAM) following a neuromuscular training (NMT) program with augmented biofeedback in individuals at high and low risk for injury. DESIGN: Secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial. METHODS: One hundred fifty adolescent female soccer players were enrolled in a 6-week NMT program and randomized to biofeedback training groups: NMT + Hip-focus (NMT+H), NMT + Knee-focus (NMT+K), or NMT with a sham biofeedback. NMT was completed 3 times each week with augmented biofeedback delivered once per week. Standard 3-dimensional motion analysis of a drop vertical jump over artificial turf with embedded force platforms was performed at baseline (PRE), immediately following training (POST), and 6 months post training (RET). Baseline measures of KAM were used to stratify participants into low- (n = 87, 12.7 ± 2.2 years, 153.0 ± 11.4 cm, 47.2 ± 11.8 kg) and high-risk (n = 44, 14.0 ± 1.8 years, 161.6 ± 5.8 cm, 53.5 ± 9.2 kg) groups, based on a previously determined cut point. A mixed-design analysis of variance with between-group factors of risk (high, low) and training group (NMT+H, NMT+K, NMT), and a repeated within-group factor of session (PRE, POST, RET) were used for the analysis. RESULTS: A significant interaction was identified between risk and session (P < .001). Within training groups, the high-risk group had a significant reduction in KAM from baseline to posttest, and from baseline to 6 months (PRE: -37.5 ± 9.0 N m; POST: -25.2 ± 11.4 N m; RET: -29.4 ± 14.5 N m). There were no changes in the low-risk group (PRE: -12.2 ± 6.2 N m; POST: -12.2 ± 7.6 N m; RET: -12.9 ± 8.7 N m). CONCLUSION: Female soccer players with knee biomechanics that put them at high risk for anterior cruciate ligament injury had improved KAM following an NMT program. The changes in KAM remained at 6 months after training. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2026;56(10):689-698. Epub 28 Aug 2026. doi:10.2519/jospt.2026.14125.

articles.title: Is plant-based protein supplementation as effective as whey protein? A systematic review and meta-analysis in untrained adults undergoing resistance training.
articles.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
articles.authors: Irineu Otavio Marchiori Callegari, Giovana Molina Silva, Alexandre Gabarra Oliveira
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Dietary protein supplements are commonly consumed to support increases in lean body mass among healthy adults engaged in resistance training (RT). Although whey protein has been extensively investigated, plant-based protein supplements have emerged as a viable alternative for individuals who avoid animal-derived products. METHODS: The present study aims to evaluate, through a systematic review and meta-analysis, the effects of plant-based versus whey protein supplementation on body composition in untrained adults (18-59 years) undergoing RT, using Dual-Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry (DEXA). The systematic review was conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 checklist and was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251145410). Searches were conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect, identifying 5 studies that met the inclusion criteria for qualitative synthesis and meta-analysis. RESULTS: When combined with RT, both plant-based and whey protein supplementation were associated with improvements in lean body mass (LBM) and body fat mass (BFM), with no significant between-group differences observed. CONCLUSIONS: Thus, soy- and pea-based protein supplements may support favorable body composition changes in adults initiating RT and could be considered practical nutritional options for individuals seeking alternatives to whey protein. Regarding chia-based protein, the available evidence is currently limited to a single study that did not demonstrate significant changes in lean body mass; therefore, firm conclusions regarding its efficacy cannot be drawn at this time.

articles.title: Hematological and biochemical responses to three doses of caffeine during the CrossFit® workout: a randomized, double-blind, crossover trial.
articles.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
articles.authors: Natalia Główka, Tomasz Podgórski, Jakub Malik et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: This study investigated the effects of three doses of caffeine (CAF) on hematological and biochemical responses during the CrossFit® workout, a protocol known to induce significant physiological fluctuations. METHODS: In a randomized, double-blind, placebo (PLA)-controlled crossover trial, 26 moderately trained CrossFit® athletes received acute doses of 3, 6, or 9 mgCAF/kgbody mass (BM), or a PLA, 70 min before a 17-min CrossFit® workout. RESULTS: While exercise was the predominant driver of hematological changes, with no CAF-specific modulation of blood cell indices, significant treatment × time point interactions were observed solely for glucose concentration. Specifically, MEDIUM (6 mgCAF/kgBM) and HIGH (9 mgCAF/kgBM) CAF doses produced significantly greater post-exercise glucose elevations compared to baseline and PLA visits. Phosphates concentrations increased over time, particularly post-exercise, with no treatment effect retained after excluding baseline visit in the sensitivity analysis. Calcium level dynamics were influenced by temporal factors rather than CAF, and magnesium concentration remained stable. CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that acute CAF ingestion selectively influences post-exercise glucose responses during the CrossFit® workout, whereas hematological variables and most biochemical markers remain unaffected. Significant post-exercise glucose elevations were observed following the 6 and 9 mgCAF/kgBM conditions compared with baseline and PLA visits, while serum mineral concentrations remained largely stable across treatments. CLINICAL TRIALS REGISTRATION: NCT03822663.

articles.title: Acute caffeine and carbohydrate strategies for fatigue-related sport-specific performance in team-sport athletes: a systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis.
articles.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
articles.authors: Shu Xie, Xueming Wen
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Although caffeine and carbohydrate are established ergogenic strategies for physical performance, it remains unclear whether these benefits translate to the decision-making and sport-specific skills that determine team-sport performance under fatigue. METHODS: PubMed, Web of Science Core Collection, and SPORTDiscus were searched on 28 July 2026. Thirty-one reports were retained; their reported analyzed sample sizes summed to 441 athletes. Twenty-three independent quantitative study clusters, with reported analyzed sample sizes summing to 341 athletes, contributed 67 effects. Multilevel random-effects models nested effect sizes within studies; primary assumptions were r = 0.5 and rho = 0.80. Inference used CR2 robust standard errors and Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. RESULTS: Soccer supplied 11 of the 23 quantitative clusters; every other sport category supplied four or fewer. Broad caffeine was centered near zero (Hedges' g = 0.040, 95% CI -0.211 to 0.291; p = 0.691; df = 4.41). Tier 1a perceptual-motor and Tier 1b technical/tactical estimates were imprecise. Broad carbohydrate was positive but uncertain (g = 0.256, 95% CI -0.094 to 0.605; p = 0.118; df = 4.96), and one study cluster materially influenced this estimate. All six GRADE comparisons were rated very low certainty. The two-study mental-fatigue calculation was too fragile for conventional inference. CONCLUSIONS: Current evidence does not support assuming that the established physical ergogenic effects of caffeine translate to fatigue-related decision-making or sport-specific skill. Carbohydrate may provide a small benefit, but the evidence remains sparse and highly uncertain. Sensitivity to study composition was driven primarily by one influential cluster, whose omission increased the pooled estimate. The carbohydrate estimates apply only to heterogeneous ingested-beverage protocols and should not be extrapolated to mouth-rinse or gel strategies. Parallel syntheses do not establish intervention superiority or combined-strategy synergy.

articles.title: Selective recovery effects of short-term beetroot juice supplementation after exercise-induced muscle damage in trained female volleyball players.
articles.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
articles.authors: Shuning Zhang, Xudong Yang, Hongqi Xu et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Beetroot juice (BRJ) has been proposed as a nutritional aid for recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD), but evidence in female team-sport athletes is limited. It also remains unclear whether any benefit extends across functional, pain-related, swelling, and strength outcomes. METHODS: Seventeen female university volleyball players entered a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial. Four did not complete the second period, so outcomes were analyzed with linear mixed models. After baseline testing, participants performed 200 loaded vertical jumps and consumed BRJ or placebo at 24, 48, and 72 h post-EIMD. Recovery outcomes were countermovement jump (CMJ) height, volleyball-specific agility time, pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, visual analog scale soreness, and knee isokinetic measures. Holm-adjusted planned contrasts were used. RESULTS: CMJ height was the clearest BRJ-related functional finding. The treatment × time interaction showed a trend toward statistical significance (P = 0.062), and CMJ height was higher under BRJ than PLA at 72 h post-EIMD (P = 0.033, d = 1.01). Calf pressure pain threshold also favored BRJ at 72 h, accompanied by a significant treatment × time interaction (P < 0.001). In contrast, agility time and soreness changed over time without clear between-condition differences, while thigh pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, and low-velocity knee isokinetic outcomes showed no consistent BRJ-related advantage. CONCLUSIONS: Short-term BRJ supplementation was associated with selective rather than generalized recovery benefits after EIMD in trained female volleyball players. The clearest findings were higher CMJ height and calf PPT under BRJ than PLA at 72 h, whereas the remaining outcomes showed no consistent treatment-related differences.

articles.title: Pre-sleep milk-derived proteins do not impair sleep or recovery in elite female athletes.
articles.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
articles.authors: Kieran G P Paterson, Timothy D Griest, Elisa Angeles et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Sleep is essential for athlete recovery and performance, yet athletes frequently experience restricted or poor-quality sleep. Pre-sleep feeding (PSF) has emerged as a strategy to support recovery, but randomized, double-blinded, crossover trials comparing PSF macronutrient options on objective and subjective sleep outcomes in elite female athletes remain limited. METHODS: Twenty-five National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I female athletes (18-25 years old) were recruited; 21 completed the trial. In a randomized, double-blinded, placebo controlled, crossover design conducted over 4-8 weeks, participants consumed four treatments for three consecutive nights each: 40 g casein protein (CAS; 160 kcal), 40 g α-lactalbumin protein (ALA; 160 kcal), 40 g carbohydrate (CHO; 160 kcal), and 40g of a placebo (PLA; 5 kcal), with a minimum three-day washout between conditions. Supplements were consumed ~2 h after the final meal and ~30 min before bedtime as the last caloric intake of the day. Objective outcomes were obtained from the WHOOP 4.0 device (total sleep time (TST), sleep onset latency (SOL), sleep efficiency (SE), resting heart rate (RHR), and heart rate variability (HRV)). Subjective outcomes were assessed each morning via questionnaires (subjective sleep quality (SSQ), subjective sleep onset latency (SSOL), and subjective recovery (SREC)). Nocturnal interstitial glucose was assessed via blinded continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) in a subset (n = 6). Sleep and recovery variables were analyzed using one-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) to evaluate treatment effects across the four supplementation conditions. For CGM data, a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA was used to evaluate main effects of treatment and time, as well as the treatment × time interaction. Tukey's post hoc testing was used with significance set at p < 0.05. RESULTS: No significant treatment effects were observed for TST, SOL, SE, RHR, or HRV (p > 0.05). TST ranged from 7.47-7.62 h, SE from 91.5-92.0%, RHR from 53.5-54.1 bpm, and HRV from 98.2-103.9 ms across conditions. No significant treatment effects were detected for SSQ, SSOL, or SREC (p > 0.05); SSQ ranged from 69-75%, SSOL from 16-20 min, and SREC from 61-66%. In the CGM sub-analysis, a main effect of time was observed for nocturnal glucose (p = 0.008), but no differences among treatments (p = 0.187) or a time × treatment interaction (p = 0.550) were detected. CONCLUSIONS: In NCAA Division I female athletes, three consecutive nights of pre-sleep ingestion of CAS, ALA, or CHO did not impair objective or subjective measures of sleep or recovery compared with PLA. These findings demonstrate that pre-sleep feeding, regardless of macronutrient type, can be incorporated without negatively affecting sleep quality or recovery metrics. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: STUDY00004409).
